Abstract
Fiber-reinforced composite (FRC) materials have gained significant traction in various industrial sectors, including aerospace, 
marine, and energy applications, owing to their outstanding mechanical properties, lightweight nature, high strength, and corro-
sion resistance. However, ensuring the reliability and durability of these materials under diverse environmental conditions, such 
as exposure to elevated temperatures, mechanical loads, and chemicals/oxidations, remains a critical challenge. In this study, we 
provide an in-depth insight into the failure mechanisms of FRC materials under several scenarios expected when in service or 
during operations, particularly for failure arising from mechanical, thermal, and chemical exposure, which are the main condi-
tions experienced in aircraft, helicopters, drones, wind turbines, and ships. Moreover, we excerpt representative cases that illus-
trate changes in material properties due to prolonged exposure to an uneven temperature gradient leading to thermal expansion 
mismatch, matrix softening, and fiber degradation. Also, a critical examination of the stress distribution, damage evolution, and 
failure criteria of FRC materials due to mechanical loads under the tensile, flexural, impact, and compressive loading conditions 
through experimental, theoretical, and numerical studies is presented to offer significant contributions to the understanding of 
failure mechanisms and their consequences for structural design and performance optimization. Thus, chemical and oxidative 
degradation in FRC materials, including matrix degradation, fiber-matrix interface debonding, and their impact on mechanical 
properties, has been analyzed. The media include aviation fuels, seawater environments, hydraulic fluids, deicer, and acidic and 
alkaline solvents. Furthermore, this work includes an overview of numerical and analytical perspectives concerning the tripod 
(mechanical, thermal, and chemical oxidations). To bring forth a series of models, theories, and assumptions employed by several 
researchers to recreate real-world applications with very high accuracy to experimental data, a detailed overview of the FRC failure 
mechanism in various environmental conditions has been reviewed, and gaps that can be explored in future research have been 
highlighted. Challenges and limitations hindering the accurate screening of composite materials for intended applications have 
been reported. It is anticipated that scholars, engineers, and researchers engaged in the development and application of the FRC 
materials in the aerospace, marine, and energy industries will find this review beneficial. It will assist them in comprehending 
composite failures under different environmental and loading conditions and provide critical insights for advancing the design, 
manufacturing, durability, and reliability of the FRC-based structures and components in the harsh operating environments.

distinct properties exhibited by these materials are required 
for many high-technology applications, such as those seen

portation industries [1–5]. For instance, biomaterial engi-
neers are increasingly looking for a structural material with 
high tensile strength, increased resistance to corrosion, low 
cost, and lightweight. The combinations of these properties 
are tough to find in a single material because materials with 
high strength or stiffness essentially have a low toughness 
[6–8]. As such, composite materials are obtained by combi-

materials. Although some composite materials naturally 
exist in nature, for example, bone is a composite of protein 
collagen and mineral apatite. Also, wood consists of cel-
lulose fibers and lignin. It goes without saying that majority 
of the composite used for numerous industrial applications 
are artificially made. A composite is a material that are made 
by reinforcement of materials with another material via a 
systematic processing approach. The two materials must be 
chemically dissimilar and separated by an interface. Depend-
ing on the nature of the reinforcement, composite materials 
can generally be classified into particle-reinforced, fiber-
reinforced, structural, and nanocomposite [9, 10]. Numerous 
combinations have been proposed by material scientists to 
produce a novel material. Majority of the created composites 
exhibit an improved combination of mechanical properties 
such as ambient and high-temperature strength, stiffness, and 
toughness.
Fiber-reinforced composites (FRCs) are classes of com-
posite materials in which the dispersed phase in the form of 
a fiber used as reinforcement and the matrix is employed as 
glue which binds them together and facilitate stresses trans-
fer between the reinforcing fibers. The main goal of FRCs is 
to obtain a material with high strength and elastic modulus 
on a weigh basis and has been identified as suitable struc-
tural materials owing to their favorable stiffness, strength, 
thermal expansion, and density properties [11]. They are 
currently used in more widespread applications ranging 
from aerospace sector to automotive, construction, vehicle/
spacecraft for space exploration, consumer products, field 
of sport, and games and replace metal components in a cor-
rosive environment, and any application where weight and 
cost reduction is an important design consideration [12–15] 
(Fig. 1). The mechanical properties of the FRC materials 
are influenced by fiber volume fraction and fiber direction. 
FRCs can be categorized into four groups based on their 
matrices: polymer matrix composites (PMCs), metal matrix 
composites (MMCs), carbon–carbon composites (C/C), and 
ceramic matrix composites (CMCs) [16] (Fig. 2). In the case 
of a polymer, resin is the matrix that is used to hold the rein-
forcement together. PMCs are typical different from other 
types due to their lightweight and can further be classified 
as thermoplastic, thermosets, and elastomeric composites. 
Curing temperature is the main factor that distinguishes ther-
moset and thermoplastics. While the thermoplastic can be 
heated further and remelted after curing, thermosets have 
crosslinked chains during curing and form stiff products that 
cannot be reshaped further after curing but perform excel-
lently at elevated temperature application due to their reten-
tion of structural rigidity at that condition. Some examples 
of thermoset polymer matrices are epoxy, polyimide, polyes-
ter, vinyl ester, phenolic, and polyurethane. However, com-
mon examples of thermoplastic matrices are polyaryletherk-
etone (PAEK), polyetherimide (PEI), polyetherketoneketone 
(PEKK), polypropylene, and polyetheretherketone (PEEK). 
The typical elastomeric material is rubber and can be 
obtained through vulcanization process. MMCs are much 
more expensive than PMCs because of the matrix materials 
(aluminum, titanium, copper, aluminum–lithium, magne-
sium, and their alloys) used. Particulates of silicon carbide 
(SiC), alumina, boron, carbon, molybdenum, and titanium 
carbides are commonly used as reinforcement. MMCs are 
relatively light in weight, thermal distortion, and wear resist-
ance and are suitable for use in automobile and aerospace 
industries, as well as electronic packaging and temperature 
regulation system [17–25]. Reinforcements employed in 
CMCs are in the form of flakes, nanofilaments, fibers, and 
nanoparticles such as carbon nanotubes (CNTs), while the 
matrix materials typically having a melting point above 
1600° are boron nitride (BN), SiC, WC, ­Al2O3, ­Cr2O3, ­ZrO2, 
­Cr2O3, and ­TiO2 and are used as cutting tools for machining 
hard metal. The C/C are relatively new and are currently 
not in use extensively. The matrix and reinforcement mate-
rials are carbon based and are typically used in aerospace 
part due to their resistance to creep, relatively high thermal 
conductivity, low thermal expansion coefficient, and high 
strength. However, they are susceptible to high-temperature 
oxidation. It should be noted that the selection of the fiber 
matrix combination, irrespective of the classes of compos-
ites, depends on the bonding strength to avoid fiber pullout 
and delamination [26–29]. Depending on the usage condi-
tions and intended application, various combinations of fiber 
and matrix materials can be used to form a hybrid composite 
template, which is a key design configuration for failure as 
dissimilar material used for the definite purpose fails at dif-
ferent times. Such composites are principally used in light-
weight air, water, and land structural components. Other 
ingredients such as fillers and additives are introduced into 
composite system. While fillers are used to replace some 
expensive constituent materials to improve some properties 
of the composite and reduce cost, additives are employed 
to impart some desirable attributes to the matrix such as

Failure is an important consideration in the design of com-
posite materials for any intending applications as its occur-
rence can put human life in jeopardy, production downtime, 
and economic losses. It is relatively difficult to prevent com-
posite failure even though its cause might be known. It is 
the responsibility of the engineers, researchers, and policy 
makers to anticipate possible failure and design appropriately 
against it. Failure of composite materials can be analyzed at 
macroscopic and microscopic levels [30, 31]. The laminate is 
viewed as a homogenous anisotropic material and fails when 
the stress levels exceed the failure criterion at macroscopic 
level. In some instances, failure of one ply does not neces-
sarily result in total failure of the laminates but affected its 
stiffness and strength. However, at the microscopic levels, 
distribution of internal stresses and load transfer between 
constituent matrix and fibers determine the total performance 
of the composite laminates [32–35]. The basic failure modes 
are compressive/tensile failure of the fibers, bond breaking at 
the fiber-matrix interface, tensile, compressive or shear frac-
ture of the matrix, matrix cracking, and delamination. These 
modes are interdependent, and the occurrence of one might 
trigger another. Failure mechanisms in the fiber-reinforced 
composite are functions of constituent materials (matrix and 
fibers), fiber orientations, state of stresses, and environmental 
conditions [36–39]. In several cases, deformations may imply 
failure; however, only total fracture or delamination accounted 
for failures in others. The difficulties arising from monitoring 
and predicting component life are because the FRCs do not 
fail by merely single crack initiation and propagation. Dur-
ing operation, damage accumulates throughout the materi-
als until a critical stage is reached where there is a complete 
separation into two or more parts [40]. The performance of 
the FRCs when subjected to various loads, including cyclic 
load, is significantly affected and could result in reduction in 
service life. Hence, it is extremely important to understand the 
fatigue behavior of the FRCs.

The failure of the FRCs during structural applications 
can be generally termed fatigue, due to its occurrence after a 
long period of repeated stresses or cyclic strain. The fatigue 
results from the change in mechanical loads, chemical or 
water ingress, service temperature, and environmental con-
ditions. As such, fatigue of composite materials is a complex 
phenomenon, as the life span of materials under repeated 
stresses are influenced by numerous variables concurrently 
[41, 42]. Also, individual deformation features of the constit-
uent. Particularly, the elastic and plastic behavior of the fiber 
and matrix determined the composite fatigue behavior. The 
characterization of failure modes is extremely difficult due to 
the number and complexity of fracture mechanism showed 
by the composite materials [43]. They may suffer varieties of 
damages during the manufacture, maintenance, and service 
life, of which low impact velocity is considered the most 
dangerous because it triggers structure strength reduction, 
although it can be viewed clearly from the component sur-
face. Composite materials failure may be catastrophic and 
difficult to predict, as evident from S–N plots of samples 
tested under similar conditions with huge differences in life 
span. As a result, it is highly important to monitor damage 
accumulations during component service lifetime to avoid 
application of large safety factors, particularly, by studying 
the component stiffness with non-destructive testing tools 
such as electromagnetic acoustic transducers (EMAT), 
ultrasonic tools (UT), and computed tomography (CT) scan 
[44–48].
Giving the intricacies of various combinations of factors 
responsible for the composite failure and the huge impact of 
failure on the economic and efficient exploitation of compos-
ite materials, numerous studies have been conducted to sim-
ulate the actual service condition of the laminated panels and 
identified main causes of failure and how it can be mitigated, 
if not completely eliminated. In some instances, unpredict-
able damage might occur due to intermittent weather condi-
tions, such as temperature changes. For instance, wind tur-
bines are exposed to the atmosphere during the service life 
and are subjected to repeated temperature changes owing to 
variations in temperature during day and night. The same is 
applicable to commercial airplanes and ships in marine envi-
ronments, though some superhydrophobic coatings are rec-
ommended in these environments due to severity of exposure 
to high salinity fluids [49]. Composites are inhomogeneous 
materials, and to develop a monitoring and life prediction 
method for these kinds of materials requires understanding 
of the failure mechanisms. Also, due to its nature, it has been 
extremely difficult to arrive at a failure mechanism that is 
suitable for all composite materials. Hence, there is a need 
for a material scientist and engineer to understand the dam-
age accumulation processes in composite.
Although there are numerous review articles in the litera-
ture that expository FRCs and its failures [50–55], however, 
none of them address the failure wholistically as this current 
paper, giving the extensive overview of failure mechanisms 
of the FRCs under different scenarios. Morampudi et al. 
[56] presented only on the mechanical properties of polymer 
matrix glass fiber and how its properties can be improved. 
Other reinforced materials such as carbon, Kevlar (aramid), 
and natural fibers were left out. Additionally, there is no 
discussion on failure modes and mechanisms. Shah et al. 
[54] focused on the factors that affect impact resistance and 
damage tolerance, emphasizing resin toughness and fabric 
structure. Wan et al. [57] recently summarize the advance of 
micromechanics-based RVE model in the FRPC. However, 
when looking closely, it can be seen that other factors, such 
as chemical failure, arise from aircraft exposure to harsh 
environments and various defects due to oxidation. Major-
ity of the review articles considered only a particular kind 
of studies. After detailed scrutiny of previously published 
articles on related topics in the literature, it is obvious that 
the current paper unravel failure mechanical in all conditions 
expected during the service life of composite materials to 
give a clearer view on initiation and propagation of cracks 
and necessary design strategies to mitigate its occurrence. 
This paper gives a comprehensive review of the FRCs failure 
due to mechanical, thermal, and chemical exposure, which 
are the main conditions which aircraft, helicopters, drones, 
wind turbines, and ships can interact with during their ser-
vice life—at the same time, trying to widen the scope by 
considering various reinforcements and matrices, test con-
ditions, and various characterization techniques. Also, a 
multidisciplinary approach combining cutting-edge experi-
mental methods, theoretical, and numerical simulations to 
unravel the intricate failure behavior of FRCs under chal-
lenging conditions were emphatically discussed. Thorough 
and comprehensive overview of FRCs failure mechanisms, 
strategies for optimized material performance, limitations, 
and possibilities for improvement of the analysis approach 
were included in this paper. A detailed insight into thermal 
failure analysis of FRCs upon exposure to elevated tem-
peratures is provided in Sect. 2, emphasizing experimental 
studies and considering the impacts of various parameters 
such as Fiber orientations, arrangement, and volume fraction 
on heat propagation in the laminate composite. Section 3 
extensively presents the failure mechanism induced by vari-
ous mechanical loadings, such as compression after impact 
(CAI), tensile, flexural, impact, compression, fatigue, and 
short beam shear. The failure behavior of the FRCs in chemi-
cal and oxidation environments was discussed in Sect. 4, 
with more focus on moisture diffusion through the fiber-
matrix interfaces when aged in seawater, jet fuel, biodiesel, 
kerosene, and water in carbon, glass, aramid, and various 
natural fibers. The detailed impact of these environments on 
the composite microsite and mechanical performance was 
highlighted. Numerical and analytical perspectives on the

2  Thermal failure analysis of fiber‑reinforced 
composites
In the manufacturing sectors, a variety of equipment made 
from composite materials are used [10, 58–65]. They can 
work in a range of temperatures, but it should be noted that 
the as the temperature changes over time, thermal stresses 
may develop at the microstructural level and weaken the 
material’s strength [66]. FRCs (particularly carbon) are pre-
dominantly used in engineering applications where there 
are high strength-to-weight ratio and low thermal expan-
sion [60]. The non-uniformity in the distribution of the 
microstructural elements in this sort of composite material 
is a problem that could result in a buildup of heat stress 
that could fail along the material interface. Additionally, 
a prolonged exposure to an uneven temperature gradient 
may cause the properties of materials to change [67]. For 
instance, carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) compos-
ite materials obtained from a thermoset matrix significantly 
degrade significantly when exposed to temperature above 
200°C [68–70]. As a result, studies on the performance of 
composite materials at elevated temperature are on the rise 
because of limited knowledge on the thermoelastic behavior. 
Therefore, it is crucial to have a full grasp of the mechanical 
behavior and high-temperature behavior of the FRP compos-
ites. Fiber orientation, arrangement, and volume fraction are 
the elements of thermoset composite materials that have an 
impact on heat propagation [71, 72]. Additionally, research 
done at cryogenic temperatures shows how microcracks 
spread at the fiber/matrix interface, causing debonding and 
delamination [73–75]. Han et al. reported that significant 
decrease in the strength and fracture strain is associated with 
thermal residual stresses which alters locations of damage 
onsets and damage evolution path [76].
Thermomechanical performance of hybrid composite 
made from various sequence of basalt and Kevlar fiber has 
been studies to ascertain the thermal stability of the speci-
men [77]. In a typical experiment, thermoplastic resin (poly-
amide-6) was used as the matrix phase. The decomposition 
of the matrix and Kevlar fiber was recorded a temperature 
range of 360 to 390°C and 500 to 580°C, correspondingly. 
The least amount of weight loss was recorded in basalt 
composite, indicating a highest resistance of thermal deg-
radation. However, hybridized samples reasonably improve 
the thermal degradation with lower weight loss. Thereby 
enhancing the overall thermal stability of the composites. 
Based on DSC analysis, hybridization and basalt show 
higher peaks of heat flow, suggesting that the thermoplas-
tic based composite materials have better thermal stability 
compared to the thermoset counterpart. Basalt composite 
and hybrid of basalt Kevlar in a particular sequence (BKBK 
&BKKB) are recommended for applications requiring high 
thermal stability.
It is important to know the thermal stability and ther-
mooxidative properties of the CFRP and its constituent ele-
ments due to fire hazard [78, 79]. Most times, composite 
characteristics, such as fiber-to-volume fraction, fiber ori-
entation, and stacking sequence, are varied to modify the 
response of the CFRP to elevated temperature and thermal 
decomposition pathways. These are mostly achieved by 
quantifying the thermal stability of the material in terms of 
weight loss and examine reactions sequence (pyrolysis and 
oxidation steps) begin and end under controlled environ-
ments with different volume fraction, matrices, and rein-
forcements. Upon completion of these processes, a clear 
understanding of the materials degradation performance and 
thermomechanical response to fire exposure. Aspinall et al. 
recently studied the thermal performance the CFRP, epoxy 
resin, and carbon fiber using a thermogravimetry method in 
two atmospheric condition at different heating rates [80]. 
The epoxy resin used as the composite matrix undergoes 
thermal decomposition after strongly resisting it up to a tem-
perature of 400°C in an oxygen-free pure nitrogen atmos-
phere. On the other hand, carbon fiber reinforcement does 
not degrade in nitrogen environment. CRFP and its con-
stituents underdo degradation through a complex reaction 
pathway consisting of three endothermic reactions (epoxy 
resin pyrolysis, residue oxidation from the first pyrolysis 
reaction, and oxidation of carbon fiber). Similarly, thermal 
degradation analysis of thermoplastic (e.g., PAEK, PEEK, 
and PEKK) based composites was presented by Tadini et al. 
[81]. The sample exhibited higher thermal performance as a 
result of its chemical structure of the monomer and as such 
its usage in aerospace application is on the rise.
The thermal behavior of the hybrid natural fiber compos-
ites carried out at a mean temperature of 55°C indicates no 
significant difference in thermal conductivity compared to 
aloe vera, and jute exhibited a less conductivity [82]. How-
ever, jute shows a better heat deflection temperature, followed 
by hybrid and then aloe vera laminates. Hao et al. found that 
the temperature increase does not influence axial modulus 
degradation [83]. However, the shear modulus is sensitive 
to temperature rise as it decreases by 20.8% at 150°C. The 
degradation of mechanical properties of a composite at ele-
vated temperature must be noted, particularly those that have 
to do with epoxy matrix. Similarly, more sensitivity of the 
transverse tensile strength degradation to temperature rise

thermally treated at 400°C showed the best tensile strength

reported an increase in the load carrying capacity of nano-
sized montmorillonite composite fiber-reinforced plates at 
200°C and 300°C exposure with changes in surface color 
on the sample from brown to black. However, there is sharp 
reduction in the fracture load, elastic modulus, and fracture

According to Lu and Xian’s research [96], persistent ten-
sile loading at high temperatures led to irreversible degrada-
tion of the fiber-matrix interface of BFRP plates due to stress 
redistribution, which significantly decreased the tensile char-
acteristics. The severity of the ensuing degradation increased 
with the exposure temperature. According to Milad et al. 
[97], the flexural and impact properties of the GFRP lami-
nated decline as temperature and exposure time rise. All of 
the laminates’ bending strengths were practically impervious 
to temperature drops below Tg (60°C), although their impact 
resistance fell by more than 10%. Additionally, Jarrah et al. 
[85] proposed the diagnostic plots based on Bayesian models 
to forecast the tensile strength of the CFRP and GFRP sheets 
with and without intumescent paint at various temperatures. 
Research on the effectiveness of FRP bars under fire condi-
tions was done by Ashrafi et al. [98]; when the temperature 
was below 90°C, the tensile strength could remain consist-
ent, but when it was above 90°C, it substantially reduced. An 
experimental examination of the mechanical characteristics 
of FRP reinforcement bars exposed to high temperatures 
has been published by Wang et al. [99]. Below 350°C, it 
was discovered that the FRP composite bars retain a very 
high percentage (90%) of their initial stiffness. The GFRP 
and CFRP composite bars’ respective strength decreases 
at 350°C are roughly 45% and 35% of their original ambi-
ent temperature strengths. Failure mechanism observed in 
alkaline-treated and alkaline-untreated banana FRCs after 
thermal characterization up to a temperature of 600°C is 
shown in Figs. 4 and 5. Tensile fracture specimen is charac-
terized with fiber fracture and pull out, while impact frac-
ture specimen experiences fiber matrix debonding and fiber 
pull out. In an attempt to mirror the service conditions of 
composite materials especially in nuclear reactor, wind tur-
bines blades, and water tanks, GFRP composite specimen 
was subjected to various mechanical tests (Tensile, Charpy 
impact) at elevated temperatures (30–70°C) and investigate 
how the temperature affect the fractured toughness, absorbed 
energy, modulus of elasticity, and tensile strength [100]. In 
a typical experiment, the resin matrix made from polyester 
materials was reinforced E-glass mat chopped strand and 
E-glass woven roving fibers and the ply arranged in [0/90] 
orientations.
Recently, Dasari et al. [102] assessed the tensile and flex-
ural behaviors of glass fiber-reinforced composites doped 
with varying content of waste carbon content at 30, 50, 70, 
and 110°C. The most significant improvement in mechani-
cal performance of the sample was recorded at 0.1 wt% of 
the dope material across almost all temperature. The failure 
mechanism on the tested sample for ambient and elevated 
temperature environment was compared. Similarly, the 
tensile and in-shear properties of plain weave fabric CFRP 
composite panels subjected to different temperature condi-
tions (ambient, 82°C, 100°C, and 120°C) was investigated 
by Barile et al. [103]. The tensile properties of the speci-
men slightly increase when the test was carried out close to 
the curing temperature and reduced by about 7.88% when 
compared with ambient temperature condition. However, as 
clearly shown in Fig. 6, a significant reduction was observed 
in the shear modulus and in-plane shear strength at higher 
temperature due to the fiber-matrix interactions. Correia 
et al. [104] conducted a thorough investigation into the 
impact of elevated temperatures up to 220°C on the ten-
sile strength of pultruded GFRP laminates. They found that 
at 220°C, tensile strength retentions were 54%. Similarly, 
tensile tests on pultruded GFRP laminates were carried out

There are at least four factors that can influence the diffu-
sion rate in a bi-component composite like CFRP. Matrix bulk, 
the interphase region before the matrix-fiber interface where 
polymer chains are pinned, the matrix-fiber interface, the fiber, 
and the fiber all have different water-diffusivity rates. Fiber

5.1  Mechanical failure analysis
Numerical and theoretical models such as classical lamina-
tion theory are employed for the analysis of the mechani-
cal properties of fiber-reinforced composites. These models 
considered the composite as a layered structure, facilitat-
ing the prediction of mechanical behavior, including stress, 
strain, and failure criteria under various loading conditions. 
By combining experimental and simulation techniques, 
researchers have worked hard over the last few decades to 
address the problem of damage tolerance in composites. 
But when it comes to predicting the residual performance 
of composites after impact—a crucial issue that has received 
a lot of attention [54]—predicting the complex and distrib-

structural performance. At present, there are two main types 
of numerical analysis methods that are used to estimate how 
composites would function following low-velocity impact: 
the equivalent damage method and restart analysis approach. 
The former approach works from a quite simple notion. The 
primary method used to determine the interior damage con-
dition of composites after an impact is non-destructive test-

starting state of the residual performance analysis model and 
the final state of the low-velocity impact model by either 
simplifying the damage zone or weakening the material 
parameters equivalently. Rozylo et al. [291] and Baluch et al. 
[292] have employed this method to forecast the remaining 
strength after an impact by simplifying the characteristics 
of damage caused by the impact on composites. They then 
transfer the damaged area onto a compression finite element

6  Challenges and future outlooks
Going by the extended use of fiber-reinforced composites in 
numerous engineering applications and various conditions, 
the materials are expected to be exposed to during their ser-
vice life; it is highly important to examine the material’s 
behavior and performance under different environmental 
conditions to ease the design decision for intended appli-
cations. The potential of the FRCs has been explored by 
scientists in various research both on laboratory and indus-
trial scales. Having carefully reviewed different approaches 
employed by experts in the field to assess the failure of the 
FRCs, it was obvious that a tremendous breakthrough has 
been achieved; still, it is crucial to acknowledge some limi-
tations posed by various techniques employed, which are 
being shed light on in this section. Hence, identifies chal-
lenges and scope for future research based on critical review 
analysis are summed up as follows:
•	 The heterogenous nature of composite materials, fiber 
orientation variations, distribution of resin, and defects 
during the manufacturing process can result in variability 
from samples. This can be particularly problematic as it 
affects the reproducibility of experimental results and 
make it extremely difficult to draw a reliable conclusion 
[417, 418].
•	 For experimental investigation, precise and thorough 
material characteristics for composites must be obtained. 
However, because composite materials are anisotropic 
and nonlinear, evaluating characteristics like modulus, 
strength, and fracture toughness can be difficult. To 
account for the various loading modes and material quali-
ties, more intricate models and criteria are needed [419].
•	 Complex damage mechanisms, such as delamination, 
fiber breakage, matrix cracking, and interfacial debond-
ing, are frequently involved in composite failure. It can 
be challenging to track various damage types’ interaction 
and propagation experimentally, particularly in situations 
involving in situ or real-time testing [420–422].
•	 It can be difficult to pinpoint the exact location of failure 
initiation in composite materials. Failure can start in the 
fibers themselves, the matrix, or interfaces like the fiber-
matrix interface. Locating the precise initiation site is 
crucial for accurate understanding of failure mechanisms 
[423].
•	 Measuring the fracture parameters and characteristics 
of composite materials can be expensive and time-con-

•	 Since premature failure is likely to occur in the matrix 
first, measuring fiber failure strength has never proven 
easy. Collaborative efforts between experimentalists and 
modelers are crucial for overcoming these challenges and 
advancing the field of composite material science.
•	 Various experimental tests on composite materials are con-
ducted according to specified standards such as ASTM, 
ISO, and CEN which have specified size for specimens, 
which may not fully capture the scale effects present in 
real-world applications. Problems with scaling can restrict 
the applicability of experimental data to larger structures 
and impair the accuracy of failure predictions.
•	 Replicating real-world loading conditions in laboratory 
experiments can be challenging. In many cases, experi-
mental setups involve simplified loading configurations 
that may not fully represent the complex loading sce-
narios experienced by composite structures in service 
[413, 423, 427].
•	 Environmental elements such as moisture, temperature 
changes, and chemical exposure are frequently encoun-
tered by composite materials, and these might have an 
impact on their failure behavior and mechanical charac-
teristics. It might be challenging to regulate and duplicate 
these environmental effects in laboratory research.
•	 Hybrid materials such as nanofiber membranes made 
from graphene, MXene, and single- and multiwalled 
CNT can be used for composite protection in extreme 
environments due to their stable electromagnetic shield-
ing and improved thermal insulation [428].
•	 Other important applications in dielectric materials use 
hybrid nanomaterials such as boron nitride, silicon car-
bide, and carbon nanotubes for introducing desirable 
conductive properties [429].
•	 For experimental testing to yield valid results, pre-
cise measurement of strains, displacements, and other 
mechanical parameters is essential. Nonetheless, uncer-
tainties can be introduced and the accuracy of experi-
mental results might be impacted by noise, measuring 
technique constraints, and instrumentation flaws [337].
•	 Experimenting with composite failure can be expensive 
and time-consuming. Significant resources and experience 
are needed to fabricate test specimens, erect experimental 
rigs, and carry out experiments. Furthermore, it can take 
a lot of time to conduct long-term durability testing to 
evaluate failure under cyclic loading conditions.
•	 Personnel and equipment are at danger of injury from 
some experimental tests involving composite failure, 
such as impact testing and high-temperature testing. To 
reduce these hazards, it is crucial to make sure that the 
right facilities and safety procedures are in place.
•	 The advent of numerical simulation method provides 
alternative cost effective techniques using commercial 
FEA package, However, due to the extreme complexity 
of the CFRP composite failure, no damage model cur-
rently in use can accurately anticipate the failure behavior 
of composites in every situation [398, 423].
•	 High-fidelity mesoscale simulation techniques are neces-
sary to anticipate progressive degradation and failure in 
composites, and they can be computationally intensive. 
Therefore, advanced numerical algorithms and reliable 
experimental data are needed to improve the accuracy of 
numerical modeling for composite failure analysis.
•	 Appropriate failure criterion selection is essential for pre-
cise forecasting. Different failure criteria are available, 
and each is appropriate for a particular type of failure 
(e.g., matrix cracking, fiber failure, debonding, delamina-
tion, and fiber waviness). Selecting the appropriate stand-
ards and being aware of their limitations is a difficult 
process.
•	 In numerical simulations, the mesh utilized to discretize 
the composite structure has a significant impact on simu-
lation accuracy. Mesh sensitivity problems can occur, 
particularly in areas with strong stress gradients, which 
might affect the solution’s convergence and perhaps 
result in incorrect predictions.
•	 Composites frequently behave multiscale, exhibiting dis-
tinct failure modes at various length scales. Accurately 
capturing this multiscale phenomenon in numerical 
models can be difficult and call for specific methods like 
multiscale modeling or homogenization.
•	 The lack of comprehensive experimental data makes 
it difficult to validate numerical models for composite 
failure, particularly for complicated failure mechanisms 
and situations. The challenge of validating models is 
increased by the lack of defined testing procedures for 
composite failure. Thorough validation studies must be 
conducted to enhance the robustness of numerical mod-
els.
•	 High performance computers are needed for robust 
numerical simulations of complex composite service 
life scenarios especially when hygrothermal and mois-
ture behavior are taking into considerations.
•	 Machine learning potentials should be explored for accu-
rate prediction of failure mechanisms and mechanical 
behavior of composites by leveraging on the numerous 
experimental and numerical data.

7  Summary
Some reviews have undoubtedly been done on the failure of 
composite materials previously in open literature. However, 
the current work employed a holistic approach to captur-
ing all the anticipated conditions that fiber-reinforced com-
posites are subjected to during the service life in various 
applications, more specifically, under mechanical, chemical, 
thermal, hygrothermal, moisture ingression, chemical, and 
oxidation. Also, experimental, theoretical, and numerical 
contemporary studies are critically reviewed and exten-
sively discussed. These have not been covered in any previ-
ously published review articles, and many research gaps that 
can be explored for improvement in research and industrial 
applications of composite materials have been identified. 
The findings from this review study can facilitate choos-
ing appropriate composite materials for aerospace, energy, 
automotive, and marine applications and help understand 
the most proper tests that can be conducted to obtain reliable 
information about composite materials.
The present article includes a comprehensive overview 
of thermal oxidative studies on fiber-reinforced composites, 
which capture the thermoelastic behavior of these materials 
in a wide range of temperatures (from cryogenic to elevated 
temperature conditions). Thermomechanical properties, 
thermal stability, and degradation of mechanical properties 
at this temperature are essential for screening the perfor-
mance of these highly important materials. In this review, 
the impact of variation of various composite constituent 
parameters such as stacking sequence, fiber orientation, and 
fiber-to-volume ratio on composite laminate subjected to ele-
vated thermal conditions are presented experimentally along 
with numerical considerations. Some reports presented 
information on the aged samples’ thermal conductivity, glass 
transition temperature, and decolorization. The authors of 
numerous surveyed articles verified their experimental data 
against the theoretical and numerical results. Some created a 
correlation model and Weibull distribution with comprehen-
sive data from their respective studies. The hybridization of 
different composite materials improved mechanical and ther-
mal response, and various composite types exhibited differ-
ent failure initiation and propagation mechanisms. Similarly, 
the mechanical response of these materials under dynamic 
mechanical loads and different aviation fluids was explored 
based on the reported information in the surveyed studies.
Before selecting a laminate composite for intended appli-
cations, detailed investigations of their behavior under static 
and dynamic mechanical loads, moisture and temperature 
are important consideration during design stage. The design 
of layered composites involves considerations of maximiz-
ing and limiting factors, such as cost. Mass reduction is a 
crucial factor in the aerospace and automotive industries for 
the purpose of minimizing energy expenses. The stiffness 
of aircraft skins is crucial in order to prevent buckling and 
restrict deformations. The thermal and moisture expansion 
coefficients are crucial in the context of space antennas to 
ensure dimensional stability. Different composite materials 
are proposed for various applications based on the compo-
sition of the constituent elements and their peculiarities. 
After thoroughly considering diverse literature with numer-
ous experimental parameters and numerical modeling, the 
behavior of composite materials under different loadings and 
environmental conditions is quite different from other mate-
rials currently used for various engineering applications. 
The mechanical properties may be tailored to meet specific 
design requirements by tunning the fibers’ choice, volume 
fraction, and alignment. The fibers and the matrix carry the 
stress distribution in composite laminates. Conventionally, 
the fiber stress is higher than the matrix stress. However, 
the strain is the same, particularly in the case of a continu-
ous fiber. Also, the fiber volume fraction is an important 
parameter that must be focused on during fabrication due 
to its impact on the mechanical response of the laminate. It 
can be seen clearly from the result obtained from the sur-
veyed articles that the tensile behavior of the composite is 
distinctly different from that of metals as the deformation 
region of the stress/strain curve experienced a sharp drop 
due to the matrix becoming plastic upon composite failure. 
Compared to other materials, composite is good in ten-
sion because of the fiber stability before fracture. The final 
composite laminates are made from different fabrics, such 
as woven fiber fabrics, unidirectional fibers, and random 
chopped fibers, and are impregnated with a polymer matrix. 
Different fiber angles/orientations have been explored in the 
open literature, with symmetrical lay-up design about center 
lamina considered suitable for best thermal and mechanical 
behavior. Different fiber types used in a composite laminate 
are influenced by the cost considerations during the design 
phase and intended sample purposes. For instance, although 
expensive, carbon fiber can be employed when high tensile 
stress is desirable, while low-cost glass fiber could be used 
when lower stress is in demand.
Fractures of the composite are characterized by fiber 
fracture, cracking, delamination, fiber-interface cracking, 
fiber pull-out, and interfacial debonding. At the fracture/
crack surface, the bonding between the fiber, and the matrix 
is significantly affected, and the load at this point is zero. 
As such, the tensile stress in the fiber is zero at the crack 
surface and rises along the fiber length due to shear interac-
tion with the matrix. The fiber types, orientations, and filler 
materials influence the fatigue behavior of the composite 
materials. The qualities of a lamina are primarily determined 
by the combination of several fiber-matrix systems and fac-
tors, such as the fiber volume fraction. Subsequently, the

be developed through the exploration of machine learning 
potentials to synergize fabrication parameters, test condi-
tions, nature of loadings, fiber-matrix type, and other vari-

composite with high level of accuracy.
Additionally, the following are the paper’s point-by-point 
concluding remarks:
•	 Through cross-validation of experiments and analyses 
conducted at various scales, the risk of damage in aero-
space composite structures has been effectively handled. 
Additionally, improvements in material systems and 
manufacturing techniques have increased the damage 
resistance of composites.
•	 Engineering applications directly benefit from the results 
of experimental failure analysis, particularly in fields like 
aerospace, automotive, and civil engineering. Engineers 
may create composite structures that are safer and more 
dependable and meet particular performance criteria by 
having a thorough understanding of failure modes and 
associated thresholds.
•	 Regardless of the nature of the composite material, it was 
generally observed that the decrease in laminate thick-
ness and increase in exposure duration led to an increase 
in the rate of decline in tensile strength.
•	 On screening different laminate types at elevated temper-
atures, laminates with unidirectional fibers show excel-
lent mechanical performance, followed by continuous 
woven fibers, and randomly distributed chopped strand 
fibers performed worst.
•	 A significant change in mechanical properties of the 
CFRP and GFRP was experienced once the composite 
sample was subjected to temperature exceeding the glass 
transition temperature (Tg).
•	 Because of matrix weakening and softening, fiber domi-
nated qualities are more heat-resistant than matrix domi-
nated properties.
•	 The incorporation of nanomaterials into fiber-matrix 
components significantly enhances the mechanical prop-
erties of composite materials. However, the fractured 
components are characterized by interfacial debonding, 
fiber pullout, and matrix drainage.
•	 The decline in mechanical strength of composite struc-
tures with increasing temperature occurs nonlinearly. 
Hence, Weibull analysis is highly important for the reli-
ability analysis of composite structures.
•	 To achieve good thermal stability, a proper curing cycle 
must be employed to prevent internal cracks and voids.
•	 Composite variable parameters such as fiber orientations, 
fiber contents, and number of plies significantly influenced 
the mechanical properties of composites with angle-ply 
layers showing the most significant reinforcing effect.
•	 The mechanical characteristics of the composites were 
improved with the addition of GO and EGO fillers. rEGO 
fillers were shown to significantly improve mechanical 
qualities; the composites’ Mode I and Mode II fracture 
toughness values rose by 65% (0.5 wt%) and 54% (0.25 
wt%), respectively.
•	 The hybrid composites showed enhanced properties 
when subjected to mechanical, thermal and other envi-
ronmental conditions such as hydrothermal, UV radia-
tion, moisture/water, chemical, and seawater.
•	 Compared to the CFRP, seawater, UV light and oxygen 
(ozone) aged GFRP has higher mechanical property deg-
radation. However, because of its high cost, the CFRP is 
not viable commercially for all kinds of applications.
•	 The failure mechanism in FRCs depends on the fabrica-
tion process and important variable parameters such as 
fiber-matrix content, stacking sequence, fiber orientation, 
matrix type, and fiber type.
•	 Fatigue behavior at lower stress level was characterized 
by fiber pullout and matrix cracking, while higher stress 
levels were characterized by crack propagation in the lon-
gitudinal direction.
•	 The application of a suggested nonlinear constitutive model 
in numerical analysis has been proven to closely match 
experimental data, indicating its efficacy in forecasting the 
performance of fiber-reinforced composite laminates.
•	 There have been reports on a number of numerical mod-
eling techniques for composite failure analysis, with an 
emphasis on addressing intralaminar damage by defin-
ing four failure modes utilizing standards like the Hashin 
model. This illustrates a variety of techniques used to iden-
tify the various fiber-reinforced composite failure modes.

Abstract: Fiber-reinforced composite (FRC) materials have gained significant traction in various industrial sectors, including aerospace, marine, and energy applications, owing to their outstanding mechanical properties, lightweight nature, high strength, and corro- sion resistance. However, ensuring the reliability and durability of these materials under diverse environmental conditions, such as exposure to elevated temperatures, mechanical loads, and chemicals/oxidations, remains a critical challenge. In this study, we provide an in-depth insight into the failure mechanisms of FRC materials under several scenarios expected when in service or during operations, particularly for failure arising from mechanical, thermal, and chemical exposure, which are the main condi- tions experienced in aircraft, helicopters, drones, wind turbines, and ships. Moreover, we excerpt representative cases that illus- trate changes in material properties due to prolonged exposure to an uneven temperature gradient leading to thermal expansion mismatch, matrix softening, and fiber degradation. Also, a critical examination of the stress distribution, damage evolution, and failure criteria of FRC materials due to mechanical loads under the tensile, flexural, impact, and compressive loading conditions through experimental, theoretical, and numerical studies is presented to offer significant contributions to the understanding of failure mechanisms and their consequences for structural design and performance optimization. Thus, chemical and oxidative degradation in FRC materials, including matrix degradation, fiber-matrix interface debonding, and their impact on mechanical properties, has been analyzed. The media include aviation fuels, seawater environments, hydraulic fluids, deicer, and acidic and alkaline solvents. Furthermore, this work includes an overview of numerical and analytical perspectives concerning the tripod (mechanical, thermal, and chemical oxidations). To bring forth a series of models, theories, and assumptions employed by several researchers to recreate real-world applications with very high accuracy to experimental data, a detailed overview of the FRC failure mechanism in various environmental conditions has been reviewed, and gaps that can be explored in future research have been highlighted. Challenges and limitations hindering the accurate screening of composite materials for intended applications have been reported. It is anticipated that scholars, engineers, and researchers engaged in the development and application of the FRC materials in the aerospace, marine, and energy industries will find this review beneficial. It will assist them in comprehending composite failures under different environmental and loading conditions and provide critical insights for advancing the design, manufacturing, durability, and reliability of the FRC-based structures and components in the harsh operating environments.
